units.title: Unit 31 — Business
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 66–67 (PDF pages 70–71).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe starting, operating and expanding a business using natural verb–noun combinations.
Distinguish business profitability, turnover, contracts and market competition.
Use idiomatic expressions for commercial success, failure and public share offerings.
Avoid learner errors such as make business and inappropriate verbs with bids or contracts.

items.pt: entrar no mundo dos negócios; começar a empreender
items.example: After five years in finance, Marta decided to go into business.
items.note: Means begin a commercial activity or career as a business owner.

items.pt: abrir uma empresa; montar um negócio
items.example: They plan to set up a business selling recycled furniture.
items.note: Set up describes establishing a new business, rather than simply working for one.

items.example: I might go into partnership with a former colleague next year.
items.note: The partnership is usually a shared commercial venture; go into partnership with someone.

items.example: The shop may make a loss during its first winter.
items.note: Business income is lower than costs; the opposite is make a profit.

items.example: The company hopes to make a profit by December.
items.note: Use make with profit and loss, not do.

items.example: An economic recession can reduce demand for luxury products.
items.note: A period of economic decline, commonly used with during or in.

items.example: Several independent shops could go under without financial support.
items.note: Informal phrasal verb for a business failing financially; no object follows under.

items.pt: encerrar as atividades; fechar por fracasso
items.example: If a business folds, its workers may need to find new jobs.
items.note: Fold means close because of business failure; the subject is a firm or business.

items.example: A supplier could go bankrupt after losing its biggest customer.
items.note: Indicates an inability to pay debts; bankruptcy has a more specific legal meaning than simply being unprofitable.

items.example: Our team hopes to win a contract with the hospital.
items.note: Win emphasises successful selection after a tender or competition.

items.example: The start-up faces stiff competition from established brands.
items.note: Stiff is a standard adjective for strong commercial competition; avoid hard competition here.

items.example: We will take on staff when the new office opens.
items.note: Take on means employ additional workers; staff is normally an uncountable collective noun.

items.pt: gerar empregos; criar postos de trabalho
items.example: The new factory could create jobs across the region.
items.note: Common with projects and policies that increase employment.

items.example: High unemployment has affected spending in the area.
items.note: High describes a large unemployment level or rate.

items.pt: números de vendas; dados de vendas
items.example: The manager reviewed the sales figures before the meeting.
items.note: Refers to numerical sales results; figures is normally plural here.

items.example: Their annual turnover rose after they expanded online.
items.note: In business accounting, turnover refers to sales revenue over a year, not profit.

items.example: We should carry out market research before opening another branch.
items.note: Carry out is standard with research; conduct market research is a more formal alternative.

items.example: The agency will conduct market research on customer preferences.
items.note: Conduct is slightly more formal than carry out in this context.

items.example: We plan to launch a new product in the spring.
items.note: Launch is used when a product becomes commercially available.

items.example: The directors firmly believe in customer service as a long-term investment.
items.note: Firmly intensifies belief; believe in can take a noun or an -ing phrase.

items.example: Excellent customer service can encourage repeat purchases.
items.note: Describes the help a business provides to its customers.

items.example: We chose this supplier because it provides reliable after-sales service.
items.note: Refers to help and support given after a product has been sold.

items.example: It takes careful planning to run a successful business.
items.note: Run means manage a company, not physically operate machinery here.

items.example: She thinks the secret of success is listening to customers.
items.note: A common expression for the main reason behind a person's or company's success.

items.pt: lançar ações de uma empresa na bolsa
items.example: The owners may float a company once it has grown large enough.
items.note: Float means offer a company's shares on the stock market, typically for the first time.

items.pt: o mercado de ações; a bolsa de valores
items.example: Investors reacted quickly to the news on the stock market.
items.note: The marketplace for buying and selling company shares.

items.pt: abrir o capital; entrar na bolsa
items.example: The directors decided not to go public this year.
items.note: Means begin selling shares to outside investors, often through a stock-market listing.

items.example: The economic crisis forced several firms to reduce costs.
items.note: Broad term for serious economic problems; a recession is one possible type of crisis.

items.example: The family business will cease trading at the end of the month.
items.note: Formal expression for a business stopping its commercial operations.

items.example: Small retailers often struggle with cut-throat competition on price.
items.note: More intense and aggressive than stiff competition.

items.example: Market forces have pushed the price of materials higher.
items.note: Refers to supply, demand and other market mechanisms affecting economic outcomes.

items.example: Some manufacturers move overseas to reduce production costs.
items.note: Means relocate activity to another country, not simply sell products abroad.

items.pt: fechar as portas; deixar de operar
items.example: The bakery might go out of business if rent increases again.
items.note: Means stop operating commercially, often because of financial difficulties.

items.pt: os negócios estão prosperando; as vendas vão muito bem
items.example: Business is booming at the new bicycle shop.
items.note: Booming means growing or performing extremely well; it does not mean just being open.

items.example: A rival company released a similar device last month.
items.note: Rival describes direct competition between organisations.

items.pt: fechar um acordo; fazer um negócio
items.example: The two firms hope to do a deal before Friday.
items.note: British usage for reaching an agreement; strike a deal is another common choice.

items.example: They managed to strike a deal despite several disagreements.
items.note: Strike a deal means reach an agreement; the past form is struck.

items.example: The seller offered a discount on the price for early payment.
items.note: The pattern is a discount on the price, usually expressed as a percentage or sum.

items.example: We must balance the budget before approving more expenses.
items.note: Arrange spending and available income so that the financial plan is sustainable.

items.pt: apresentar uma proposta; participar de uma licitação
items.example: We will put in a bid for the maintenance contract.
items.note: A bid is a formal offer to win work or buy an asset; put in is the typical verb.

items.example: Our company wants to do business with local suppliers.
items.note: Use do business, not make business; do business with an organisation or person.

items.example: They submitted a competitive bid for the maintenance contract.
items.note: A bid is competitive when its terms compare favourably with rival offers.

items.pt: ganhar o contrato; vencer a licitação
items.example: A smaller engineering firm could win the contract this time.
items.note: The fixed verb is win, not earn or achieve, in the contract-selection context.

items.example: She built a successful business from a small home office.
items.note: Successful business describes a firm that meets its goals or performs well; run is the common verb.

items.example: Negotiations led to a business deal with the distributor.
items.note: Deal refers to an agreement between parties, often involving trade.

sectionsChecked: Text and footnote glosses on business failure, market research, turnover and flotation

units.title: Unit 32 — Academic writing 1: giving opinions
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 68–69 (PDF pages 72–73).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Topics: Work and study · academic writing and opinions
learningObjectives: Report, assess and challenge academic research using conventional collocations.
Distinguish strong evaluative claims from cautious or qualified statements.
Use precise structures for evidence, arguments, theories, source acknowledgement and plagiarism.
Write original short academic statements with natural verbs and appropriate prepositions.

items.example: The team expects to publish research results later this year.
items.note: Publish makes findings available formally, often in an academic journal.

items.example: Their groundbreaking research changed how the disease was studied.
items.note: Strong positive evaluation suggesting important new discoveries.

items.example: This study could make a significant contribution to materials science.
items.note: Contribution is followed by to when naming the field or objective; significant expresses importance.

items.pt: apresentar um argumento de forma organizada
items.example: The introduction should set out an argument clearly.
items.note: Set out means explain an argument systematically, not merely mention it.

items.example: The author gives powerful arguments for better public transport.
items.note: Powerful is natural with arguments; mighty arguments is not the usual academic expression.

items.example: These findings may shape our thinking about climate policy.
items.note: Shape describes a lasting influence on how people understand an issue.

items.example: The researcher continued to strenuously defend a theory that others questioned.
items.note: Strenuously signals vigorous defence against criticism.

items.pt: ser alvo de críticas; sofrer ataques
items.example: The proposed model may come under attack if new data contradict it.
items.note: In academic writing, the attack may consist of criticism rather than physical action.

items.example: Access to education can play a central role in social mobility.
items.note: Role normally combines with play, not perform, in this sense.

items.example: The report does not go into great detail about the equipment design.
items.note: Go into detail means discuss something thoroughly; great increases the extent.

items.example: You need reliable data to support an argument about safety.
items.note: Support connects a claim or argument with justification or evidence.

items.example: The historian will give an account of the events that led to the conflict.
items.note: Formal way of describing or reporting events or ideas.

items.example: The experiments provide evidence for the new hypothesis.
items.note: Provide is a neutral academic verb; the evidence does not necessarily prove the claim conclusively.

items.pt: fundamentar uma afirmação; sustentar uma alegação
items.example: The authors use survey data to support a claim about working conditions.
items.note: A claim should be supported with reasoning, observations or other evidence.

items.example: Readers may seriously misinterpret the findings without context.
items.note: Seriously intensifies a major error of interpretation.

items.example: The report begins with a concise summary of its main findings.
items.note: Concise means brief but sufficiently informative, rather than simply incomplete.

items.example: The review discusses the present state of research on sustainable energy.
items.note: A formal expression for describing how a field stands at the current time; the phrase can be followed by different subjects.

items.pt: estabelecer uma relação; demonstrar uma conexão
items.example: Researchers tried to establish a connection between sleep and memory.
items.note: Establish a connection requires supporting reasons or evidence; it need not prove causation.

items.example: The inspection found no physical damage to the device.
items.note: Damage is uncountable in this meaning; use damage to something.

items.example: The results are promising, but they do not amount to irrefutable proof.
items.note: A very strong expression for evidence that cannot reasonably be contradicted.

items.example: The charts reveal significant trends in energy consumption.
items.note: Significant can refer to an important or statistically meaningful pattern; context decides.

items.example: Reliable power is a key factor in the system's performance.
items.note: Strongly identifies an especially important contributing factor.

items.pt: um exemplo perfeito; um exemplo que ilustra exatamente
items.example: This case is a perfect example of why calibration matters.
items.note: Stronger and more categorical than a typical or useful example.

items.example: Leaders sometimes make a misjudgement under pressure.
items.note: Refers to an incorrect assessment or decision; make is the conventional verb.

items.example: Poor maintenance can have serious long-term effects on reliability.
items.note: Long-term modifies effects; serious states that consequences matter greatly.

items.pt: uma demonstração clara; um exemplo esclarecedor
items.example: The graph provides a clear illustration of the seasonal pattern.
items.note: A formal way of saying something demonstrates a point convincingly.

items.example: The article argues for a strong monetary policy during inflation.
items.note: Strong here evaluates the policy's firmness or effectiveness, not physical power.

items.pt: uma explicação provisória; uma explicação ainda incerta
items.example: The researchers offered a tentative explanation for the unusual readings.
items.note: Tentative warns that an explanation is provisional rather than firmly established.

items.pt: apoiar em linhas gerais a opinião de que
items.example: The survey results broadly support the view that flexible hours improve satisfaction.
items.note: Broadly expresses substantial but not necessarily complete agreement with a position.

items.example: The data show a strong tendency towards higher use in winter.
items.note: Tendency describes a recurring pattern, which is not always universal.

items.example: We need to gather evidence before drawing a conclusion.
items.note: Gather is standard with evidence, particularly at the beginning of an investigation.

items.example: The institute will carry out a detailed study of sensor errors.
items.note: Carry out is a natural verb for doing a study or investigation.

items.pt: desempenhar um papel em; contribuir para
items.example: Temperature may play a part in the variation we observed.
items.note: Often indicates one contributing cause among several.

items.example: The report must offer supporting evidence for its recommendations.
items.note: Supporting evidence backs up a position; it need not be definitive proof.

items.example: New measurements could challenge a theory accepted for decades.
items.note: Challenge means question or dispute a theory using arguments or evidence.

items.example: She plans to put forward a theory about the origin of the signal.
items.note: Put forward means propose for consideration, not prove.

items.example: Our group hopes to propose a theory that explains the unexpected pattern.
items.note: Formal alternative to put forward a theory; avoid give a theory.

items.example: You must acknowledge your sources in every academic report.
items.note: Means credit the work or information you have used; exact style depends on the publication.

items.example: Copying another person's text without attribution can mean you commit plagiarism.
items.note: Commit is the normal verb with plagiarism; it means dishonestly presenting others' work as your own.

items.example: Graduate students often do research alongside their coursework.
items.note: Use do research, not make research; research is normally uncountable.

items.example: Our laboratory will carry out research on vibration control.
items.note: A more formal way of saying do research; research remains uncountable.

items.example: The reviewers were convinced by an argument supported by reliable data.
items.note: Use convinced by to identify the reasoning or evidence that persuaded someone.

items.example: The journal published a fascinating study of ancient trade routes.
items.note: Fascinating evaluates an investigation as especially interesting, not necessarily conclusive.

items.pt: fundamentar uma ideia; sustentar uma hipótese
items.example: The team used measurements to back up an idea from an earlier paper.
items.note: Back up means support with evidence or explanation; common in less formal academic discussion.

items.example: The editor praised an outstanding article on battery degradation.
items.note: Outstanding is strong positive evaluation of quality.

items.example: Her thesis includes original research on feedback control.
items.note: Means research that produces new findings, not merely a review of existing publications.

items.example: The researchers will conduct a controlled experiment with two groups.
items.note: Conduct is a formal verb for organising and performing experiments.

items.example: The evidence helped the author develop a coherent theory.
items.note: Coherent means logically consistent and clearly connected.

items.example: The study aims to develop a coherent theory of the observed behaviour.
items.note: Develop means build and refine an explanation; coherent refers to logical consistency.

items.example: The university plans to undertake a comprehensive survey of graduates.
items.note: Undertake is a formal alternative to carry out; comprehensive means wide-ranging.

items.example: A comprehensive survey revealed differences between the regions.
items.note: Survey can mean a questionnaire-based investigation or broad systematic review.
